speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Today, premises which are used as hospitals, medical clinics, nursing homes and clinical laboratories in Singapore are licensed under the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act (PHMCA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: PHMCA was enacted in 1980 and sets minimum standards for licensees' premises, personnel as well as processes to safeguard patient safety and welfare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: PHMCA was last amended in 1999, and the regulatory framework needs to be refreshed and updated to address today's rapidly-evolving healthcare landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While Singapore has one of the longest life expectancies in the world, there has also been a rise in the number of unhealthy years lived because of ageing-related illnesses and chronic diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, to provide more appropriate and accessible healthcare to our ageing population, there needs to be a shift in care models to align ourselves with one of my Ministry's "Three Beyonds" – "Beyond Hospital to Community".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There will, therefore, be more vertical and also horizontal integration across traditional healthcare settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, nursing homes may now be able to also provide dementia care and geriatric clinical services within one location.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: And that is for the better, because it puts the related and complementary services under one umbrella.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These integrated models of care are difficult to license under the present premises-based licensing framework of PHMCA and, therefore, the licensing framework will need to be improved to accommodate such new and also evolving models of care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This may be possible today when hospitals or medical clinics provide telemedicine or mobile medical services, on top of their premises-based care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In other words, they provide premises-based care and, on top of that, also provide telemedicine or other mobile medical services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is, therefore, a need to move beyond just regulating premises or to be premises-based in the regulation framework, to also be able to look at regulating services delivered beyond the premises, if we want to ensure the safe delivery of such services into the community or done remotely, as I have mentioned, through telemedicine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At the same time, we also need to ensure that the welfare and well-being of vulnerable individuals or patients can be enhanced, and that the elderly and the frail patients are well looked after.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This will include the assurance for the continuity of care for patients, and the introduction of additional safeguards to prevent abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is, therefore, a need to have an enhanced governance structure to more closely monitor and also track the delivery of such newer services, including looking after the appropriateness of care and the information that is being provided to patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This Bill will, therefore, seek to achieve a few objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Third, to strengthen continuity of care and ensure more appropriate and robust licensee accountability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In putting up this Bill, the Ministry of Health (MOH) conducted extensive public and stakeholder consultations between 2017 and 2018, and also studied developments in the local landscape, as well as the regulatory regime that exists in several overseas jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We received a lot of useful feedback from licensees, patients and the public, and some of these ideas have been incorporated into the new regulatory regime that now finds its way into this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Some examples include the bundling of specific licences for general practitioners (GPs) to accommodate their core work, as well as allowing licensees to co-locate with certain registered healthcare professionals to facilitate the provision of complementary healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will clearly define the scope of the regulatory regime and the move towards a services-based licensing framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The scope of the Healthcare Services Bill extends to the regulation of any service by direct providers of "healthcare services" as defined in clause 3.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes services that diagnose, assess or treat diseases or illnesses; provide nursing or rehabilitative care; or assess the health of individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Services that will require licensing will be set out in the First Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Licensable services are largely similar to the services already provided by the premises-based licensing regime currently under PHMCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While the scope of the Bill is broad enough to include standalone allied health, nursing, traditional medicine and also complementary and alternative medicine services, we will not, at this stage, be licensing these services for the time being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, my Ministry will continue to closely assess these services, particularly from the perspective of risks to patient safety and welfare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: If sufficiently serious concerns arise, these services can then be licensed by including them in the First Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In that case, the same regulatory regime as is now set out in the Bill would then apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: They are bound by internal Government standards and rules, which are generally equivalent to or more stringent than the current licensing standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There are also staff disciplinary frameworks to deal with errant personnel in the case of such Government services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Bill's scope also does not include beauty and wellness services as these services do not diagnose, assess or treat diseases or illnesses and are of minimal patient safety risk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Entities that do not provide direct patient care, such as Third Party Agents referring patients to healthcare services licensees for their care, will also not be regulated as licensees under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: But this would be an area that we will review, and at the appropriate juncture, if necessary, can always include into the Bill through suitable amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This approach will better suit the business models of providers, who would just have to take the licences based on the services that they wish to provide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, a provider can decide if he wants to hold a suite of service licences for a nursing home, a clinic, telemedicine and health screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: That, ultimately, is the raison d'etre behind this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes, but is not limited to, whether the applicant is a suitable person and his ability to provide clinically, as well as ethically, appropriate patient care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Other factors that may also be considered include the applicant's prior conduct when participating in various public schemes, such as the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), MediSave or MediShield Life schemes, as well as the track record of compliance with regulatory requirements under the Bill and also under other laws relevant to the provision of healthcare services in a safe and appropriate manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 23 also requires the key appointment holders of a licensee, such as its governing board or key management, to be suitable persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Key appointment holders must possess the appropriate skills and competencies to carry out effective governance functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While the licensee is ultimately accountable for overall compliance to the Bill, clause 24 requires the licensee to appoint a suitably qualified individual as the licensee's Principal Officer (PO) or the Clinical Governance Officer (CGO), to strengthen accountability as well as clinical oversight at the different layers of its management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, even as powers and responsibilities are set out under the different layers of governance under the Bill, healthcare professionals will be given autonomy to exercise discretion in the execution of clinical decisions for patient care, to serve the patient's best interests and also in accordance with professional ethics and considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will, therefore, introduce provisions in the regulations for due consideration to be given to the views of practising professionals for clinical care matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 25 of the new Bill will also require certain licensees providing higher patient risk services, for example, acute hospitals, to set up specific internal committees to monitor the quality as well as the ethics of the services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These specified committees include the Quality Assurance Committees, the Service Review Committees and the Clinical Ethics Committees, each dealing with different aspects of clinical, ethical and quality considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Procedural details for these committees will be carried in the Regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Stakeholders had raised concerns on whether these governance requirements impose additional burden on smaller licensees, such as the GP clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is a relevant concern, but this will not be the case, as the requirements that are set out are appropriately calibrated to the scale and also to the complexity of the licensee's operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In addition to setting up proper governance structures and imposing standards on key appointment holders, we also need to ensure that the employment of healthcare workers – those who work or who are employed by the licensees and who deal with patients on a day-to-day basis – are also properly managed and there is appropriate oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This, I would say, is especially so when catering to the vulnerable patient groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Such patients may be at risk of abuse, particularly when they require substantially long stays at a healthcare institution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We understand that we should not treat all past offenders in the same way, or to assume that they are automatically recalcitrant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I would add that this employment restriction is not new.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is similar in nature to the approach taken under the Early Childhood Development Centres Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Additionally, the employment restrictions will be limited only to settings where patients are at higher risk if they require, for instance, substantially long stays or are mentally and physically vulnerable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This would include long-term residential care services like nursing homes, inpatient palliative care services, and the Institute of Mental Health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 29 will enhance naming restrictions to provide better clarity to patients on the healthcare services provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, non-licensees will not be able to use names that create a misimpression of providing licensable healthcare services when they either are not or should not be doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Likewise, licensees will also be prohibited from using names of services that they are not licensed to provide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 30 will disallow unrelated, unlicensed services to co-locate with or within a licensed service, unless MOH approves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The intent behind this is to prevent or, as far as possible, mitigate public misperception that such unlicensed services, such as wellness and spa services, are either endorsed or licensed, because of their close physical proximity and association with the licensed healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 31 will strengthen the advertisement controls under the Bill to prevent non-licensees from advertising licensable healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Therefore, only licensees and authorised persons appointed by a licensee will be allowed to advertise licensable healthcare services and, in doing so, will have to comply with the prescribed requirements to prevent advertisements that are false, misleading or laudatory and lead to a consumption of unwarranted treatments; and also those that cause a mismatch of expectation between the advertisement and what the public sees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Besides having levers to regulate the licensees, the Bill will also enhance existing powers of the Ministry, carried at clause 36, to gather data for patient safety, welfare and public interest purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 37 will then empower the Ministry to publish information acquired in the course of administering this Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In this regard, we intend to publish a list of non-compliant licensees and unlicensed providers, and we hope that by making such information available to the public, we can help patients make more informed decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Part 4 of the Bill will specifically introduce provisions to achieve this by empowering MOH to directly "step -in" or appoint a "step-in" operator to take over the operations of a licensee who is in serious financial trouble, or is contravening or is not complying with the provisions of the Bill, or is otherwise carrying on its operations in a manner that is detrimental to the interests of patients or customers, but nonetheless wants to or persists in carrying on these operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The primary purpose is to protect patients’ safety and welfare against a recalcitrant provider endangering patients and also preventing an abrupt discontinuation of residential healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For this reason, the "step-in" provisions will only apply to a list of designated residential healthcare entities that will be prescribed in the regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These will include nursing homes, hospitals and inpatient palliative care centres. "Stepping-in" will also be a temporary arrangement until the service has been stabilised, and the patient's safety and welfare are no longer compromised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I would add that "step-in" powers are not unique to this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Other regulatory frameworks for essential services, such as those in the financial services or transport sector or the like, also provide similar powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: And I would argue that the case for this is perhaps even more compelling in the healthcare setting, given that lives as well as the continued delivery of care to patients, whose welfare and interests are at risk, remain at stake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 39 provides powers to stop the provision of services that are detrimental to patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While such powers presently exist in PHMCA, they are limited to cases where the service endangers the health, safety and welfare of patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under the Bill, we will also be able to stop services that go against the rules of professional conduct and ethics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: So, for instance, if a disciplinary tribunal under the Singapore Medical Council has found that a particular treatment should not be provided for specific indications as there is insufficient clinical basis or evidence, MOH can issue stop orders for all licensees to cease any provision of such treatment accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To exercise oversight and control over non-compliant licensees, we will have a wider range of regulatory actions and higher penalties for offences in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 20, therefore, allows various regulatory actions to be taken against non-compliant licensees, as opposed to PHMCA, where we could only revoke or suspend the licence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: So, there is a broader range in the toolkit which allows for more flexible arrangements, given the nature of each particular situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Penalties for offences have also been updated and aligned with comparable offences under other more recently enacted legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, let me turn to the proposed implementation of this new regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The second phase will involve medical clinics and other ambulatory care services, as well as ambulance services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH will assist all licensees and ensure a seamless transition to the new licensing regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will also continue streamlining our regulatory processes to reduce the burden on licensees as far as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We strive to enable new and innovative healthcare service models as well as the use of technology to develop within safe and reasonable boundaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Healthcare Services Bill will allow my Ministry to evolve its regulatory framework in tandem with the changing needs of healthcare demands and also the changing healthcare landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Together, we can achieve the key objectives of protecting patient safety, welfare and also assuring continuity of care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: My Ministry remains committed to ensure that healthcare in Singapore is safe, of good quality, affordable, as well as accessible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As we continue to build on our regulatory transformation journey to enable new healthcare services and care models to support our ageing population, I would like to urge the Members of this House to give your support to the Healthcare Services Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a major and necessary transition, which will accommodate newer healthcare services and also healthcare delivery modes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only will this new licensing structure enable the Ministry to better regulate and govern our growing healthcare sector, it also facilitates innovation while offering patients better protection.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And how are we helping our licensees to meet the expected costs?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there also a significant difference between the regulatory costs to MOH and the licence fees and, if so, who is paying for this gap?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I seek the Minister’s assurance that costs for healthcare providers will not be increased inordinately such that patients are the ones that end up paying for this shortfall.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if for some reason under the new structure, certain licensees’ fees are, in fact, reduced, would the Ministry consider measures which will encourage such savings to be passed on to patients?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In regard to co-location of services, I would like to seek clarifications over what determines whether co-location with non-licensees will be permitted.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the continuing push from healthcare to health, I think the demarcation between health and wellness services continues to be blurred.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since we are talking about new paradigms in healthcare, what about digital providers?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, if you provide a telemedicine platform, how do we regulate how these services co-exist in the digital sphere?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would also like to ask how the Ministry intends to deal with certain service entities, such as ambulances and also standalone telemedicine providers, under this new regulatory framework.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I had previously voiced my concerns about the costs and level of expertise of private ambulance providers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, will there be stipulations regarding the construct and equipment on board medical transport and emergency ambulance vehicles?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How about the training qualifications and expertise of the personnel providing such services?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Government regulate the range of their charges and also their fees?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Users of such services, we note, are usually in a vulnerable state and are in an unfavourable position to research, compare and negotiate fees.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for telemedicine, it is a service which can be provided from anywhere to anyone so long as there is an Internet connection.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This remote medical service will attract many new providers and big information technology (IT) conglomerates to this sector.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will the Ministry ensure the quality and integrity of such services so as to safeguard our patients?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are so many aspects which have to be considered and made clear.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, under which circumstances would a medical professional be permitted to make a diagnosis and prescription remotely, and when should such face-to-face interactions be required?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What about the liability risks for practitioners in telemedicine?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And would inter-country services be allowed and under what sort of regulatory framework?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another area of concern which has been brought up in the past is how this Bill would deal with Third Party Administrators (TPAs) and medical concierges, although I do note that these do not fall within the scope of this particular Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, both provide some form of healthcare-related services by referring patients to designated or to preferred providers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, this is discouraged under the Code of Ethics, which also limits their application, but there is presently no law which specifically regulates their use.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we strive to become a Smart Nation, a unified electronic health record is a critical step towards a truly future-ready healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The hacking of the SingHealth computer system has understandably led to a pause in this regard, but it should not inflict a mortal blow to our efforts to have a robust and comprehensive digital health record system which will have many benefits for all Singaporeans, both in sickness and in health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On this note, would the Minister share an update on the measures MOH will implement to ensure that licensees protect health information in medical records?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Going digital and implementing NEHR will enhance continuity of care for patients and boost productivity, but patients understandably are also more concerned about their data privacy and their data protection.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the past, one had to physically break into a clinic or hospital to steal patient data.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, these crimes can be conducted far, far away from their targeted victims and many more patients’ data can be obtained in one fell swoop.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the macro level, how then are we fortifying our digital defences to keep up with and keep out fast-evolving cyberattacks on our databases?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the ground, how is MOH working with individual licensees to boost their cybersecurity?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, there are a variety of new services since then on offer and things have changed, for example, medical transportation, video conferencing, teleconferencing and even tissue and bone banking.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As it will usually be identified or linked to an individual, will it be under the name of the mother or the baby or the fetus?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister comment and elaborate on the offering of House Visits services by GP and Family Practitioner colleagues, for example, as well as home care services by hospice doctors and nurses?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In that same context, are there any requirements for locum healthcare services staff who move from premises to premises offering services and taking care of patients with consultations?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, pertaining to telemedicine, can the Minister also clarify with some details?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How about when our medical staff are consulted on the regional and international platforms?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At Singapore General Hospital, for example, we provide Maritime Medical Advice or Radio Medical Advice to ships in the waters around Singapore and even as far as the coverage of parts of the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Please advise on the definition and coverage of these services as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourthly, on clause 26, pertaining to the Clinical Ethics Committee (CEC), can we understand a bit more on this and also the component members and how many members will the CEC have?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, will there be any difference in the components and also job scope as compared to the Ethics Committee that our institutions already have today?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fifth, how fast can the "step in order" or the "expedited step in order" be approved and obtained in the event that it is required?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Sixth, can the Minister also explain with some details of the Quality Assurance Committee?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are the main objectives and desired goals and how will they function?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is especially so with the current economic climate, as we update this Bill to execution.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Eighth, pertaining to the process of mapping services at the healthcare premises, how fast can the request for new services be processed?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, will the spectrum of point of care tests permissible be reviewed from time to time to incorporate the latest and the updated?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is because I feel that this can be a potential area for abuse and also misinterpretation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Take, for example, the beauty and wellness industry.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is not within the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But these are exactly some of the services which may potentially co-exist on the same premises as a licensed service.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, therefore, there could be some loopholes there.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I do support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I note that MOH has proceeded cautiously in presenting this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the MOH website, it started consulting on this matter in 2016 and published a draft Bill two years ago for scrutiny and feedback.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill today is quite different from the draft Bill in some respects, which the Senior Minister of State explained briefly earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I agree that Government oversight of healthcare services is necessary to protect patient welfare, I have some queries and concerns about the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These concerns relate to the Bill's phased coverage, price transparency, quality assurance and the NEHR system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And earlier, the Senior Minister of State did explain that Government-provided services included those under the Singapore Armed Forces and the Singapore Civil Defence Force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I take it that restructured hospitals, polyclinics and also primary care providers will be covered under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is a question of at which phase they are included.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Again, related to the issue of coverage, I was originally a little puzzled by the First Schedule because it stated only certain specific types of healthcare services which will be required to licensable, particularly clinical support services and some specialised laboratory-type services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like him to confirm that emergency ambulance services and such related conveyance services would be actually included for regulation under phase 2.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, do I take it then that with regard to private ambulance services, this would be actually done under phase 2?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If that is the case, then when would that be done?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And in the meantime, would there be anything put in place to protect consumers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, are we still relying on the Voluntary Accreditation Scheme to try to get some standards into that industry?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I move on to the important issue of quality assurance for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill states upfront in the explanatory statement and the Minister also mentioned earlier that one of the Bill's aims is to strengthen safeguards for the safety and welfare of patients who receive healthcare services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since the day I became an elected Member of Parliament nine years ago, I have, from time to time, come across families who have been devastated by unsuccessful medical procedures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of their family members died unexpectedly while others sustained permanent disability in their prime and have been lying in rehabilitation hospitals for years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, it must be said that the cause of such tragic outcomes may not be the inadequacy of healthcare services but other causes, such as the nature of the illness itself or inherent risks of certain medical procedures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, healthcare is an area where there is asymmetry of knowledge, with patients placing high trust in professionals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is critical that the public must be assured that investigations into complaints are fair to the consumer and independent of professional and institutional interests.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, professionals need justice as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And we recall the High Court's decision in July last year to reverse the conviction on an orthopaedic specialist by the Singapore Medical Council.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, can the Senior Minister of State elaborate on how this Bill will enhance confidence in the fairness of the quality assurance processes for all parties?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My final point, Sir, concerns the implementation of the NEHR system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that during the public consultation on the Bill, a lot of time was spent dealing with the issue of potential data leaks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is understandable in view of recent incidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry please update the House on the status of this opt-out option?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 5.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.55 pm until 5.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the 39 years since PHMCA was enacted, the healthcare landscape has seen significant changes, including a shift towards digital and online services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, Singapore faces an ageing population and an increased prevalence of chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The demand for healthcare services is set to increase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, there is a growing need for alternative models of care beyond face-to-face consultations or healthcare provision at physical, brick-and-mortar locations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot take for granted Singapore's high-quality healthcare infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The service-based licensing model will help ensure that people in Singapore continue to have access to safe and well-regulated healthcare services, even as the services take on alternative forms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, plans to mandate the contribution of data to NEHR have been in the news as early as 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, these plans were deferred in the wake of the SingHealth cyberattack in 2018, which highlighted the risks posed by weak spots in the system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Since then, disciplinary action has been taken against top management and key individuals, NEHR has been subject to reviews, and Minister Gan Kim Yong has assured this House that the Ministry is "taking many precautions" to ensure that the system is "robust before everyone is required to submit (data)".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has also said it will implement safeguards to ensure the confidentiality of patients' NEHR records.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include the provision of access logs to patients, regular audits on NEHR access and penalties for unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as with all electronic databases, NEHR faces a risk of data breach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From a national security perspective, it would also be dire should NEHR data fall into the wrong hands.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On an individual level, patients may fear having their sensitive medical information leaked since this could have repercussions on their employment prospects or social lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the use, access and transfer of patient data will be monitored by the system?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, how will the Ministry seek to prevent abuse of authority by healthcare professionals who have access to the system?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what recourse is available for a patient who suspects that there was unauthorised access to their records?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that patient subsequently suffers perceived injustice at his or her workplace or discrimination by his or her insurer, what recourse is available then and on whom does the burden of proof fall?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Who would bear the costs of any follow-up action?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, given the concerns with data privacy and protection, there are understandable reasons why certain patients may not want their data uploaded onto NEHR.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These patients must submit a request to the Ministry, and requests will be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the criteria for assessing these requests?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be possible for the Minister to decline a patient’s request and, if so, on what grounds?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that there must be a balance and must be struck between encouraging participation in NEHR and upholding patient choice and confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide assurance that the opt-out process will not be unduly difficult for patients?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what measures are in place to ensure that the opt-out process is relatively quick and easy for patients?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide an estimate of how long the review and opt-out process might take?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, under the Bill, the licensing regime for healthcare service providers will transition from a premise-based to service-based one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, an establishment might require multiple licences depending on the services provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide some details about the projected costs for this transition?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would establishments which offer more than one type of healthcare services now have to foot higher administrative costs because they will need to hold more licences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there are any increase in costs, can the Minister clarify the proportion of the burden that will be borne by the end-user, the service provider, and the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether there will be efforts to streamline the licence application process for establishments that might require multiple licences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the Bill has step-in provisions relating to residential care services, such as hospitals, nursing homes and in-patient palliative care services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, section 33 provides that the Minister has the power to issue a step-in order.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how and when this power will be exercised?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister have access to a committee of industry experts who may be able to advise him on such matters?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a necessary move to adapt our legal framework to the rapidly evolving healthcare landscape, so as to continue ensuring the well-being and care of the people in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, it places us in a better position to embrace even more novel models of care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the above queries will aid in sharpening Singapore’s approach to the provision of healthcare services, thus securing Singapore’s continued leadership in healthcare globally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I do have a few questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The introduction of Industry 4.0 and fifth generation (5G) telecommunications are already beginning to disrupt existing modes of healthcare delivery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: New healthcare services can now be delivered entirely through mobile and online channels.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry provide licensees with a way to cluster and package their applications, to help them manage their licensing costs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should bear in mind that the end-consumers would inevitably bear the brunt of any cost increase, and businesses often have an easy excuse to raise prices once regulatory costs increase.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if the switch to the new framework will only result in an increase in licensing costs for a small number of operators, there is still a strong case to be made for the Ministry to consider absorbing the increase, as it is not uncommon to see prices increase across the industry just because someone in the market has raised their charges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The sandbox will be beneficial to help us in adapting our regulations as telemedicine technologies evolve.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The introduction of 5G technology will see telemedicine and tele-surgical services become the next key growth drivers in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Already, news reports out of China have emerged, claiming that doctors in the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) General Hospital have carried out China's first 5G-based remote surgery on a patient 3,000 kilometres away.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure that it is only a matter of time before such technologies are trialled here in Singapore, and having our own telemedicine regulatory sandbox will help strengthen our position as one of the leading healthcare hubs in the region.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, new technologies will also bring about new questions pertaining to liability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) revolutionising how illnesses are diagnosed, will our sandbox regulations differentiate between decisions made by human doctors and those made by AI?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, who will be liable for decisions made by AI?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With this sandbox, we have the opportunity to actively shape telemedicine regulations and answer the tough questions surrounding AI-related liability questions in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Ministry to do so, so that we can pave the way for our businesses to remain as innovative leaders in the region.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another opportunity for adaptive regulations under this Bill is to create a sandbox for the regulation of the entire spectrum of professions which provide Mental Healthcare Services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Industry practitioners within the mental healthcare space, such as psychologists and psychotherapists, have been providing me with feedback on their wish for the entire industry to be fully regulated as a healthcare service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From what I can understand, only psychiatrists are fully regulated today, as they are considered doctors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But mental healthcare services span across a wide spectrum of professions, many of which lack full regulations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although classified by the Ministry as allied health professionals, psychologists are yet to be regulated under the Second Schedule of the Allied Health Professionals Act which was passed in 2011.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other professions within this industry that are unregulated include counsellors and psychotherapists.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lack of regulation among the many professions within the industry is troubling, as members of the public do not know the differences between counsellors and psychologists, and may seek treatment from someone without the proper certification and expertise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should support the industry's call for fuller regulations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could consider regulating the entire industry as an allied health service under a sandbox, to be implemented in the final phase of the Act's implementation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to work with the Ministry to engage mental healthcare practitioners working across the entire spectrum of the mental healthcare industry, and work towards drafting the implementation and regulatory details, and to park this under a sandbox regime to provide all parties with the necessary flexibility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially vital for medium and large corporations which are responsible for the healthcare delivery of tens and hundreds of thousands of patients every year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, while bigger companies will be able to easily adapt to the new governance measures, smaller players, such as our local GPs will find it much harder to comply.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the new measures, licensees must appoint those with the appropriate skills and competencies in the areas of finance and business management.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will GPs be allowed to double, or even triple-hat, as the Licensee, Principal Officer and Clinical Governance Officer?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another new area of regulation which may impact smaller players more disproportionately than larger players is in private ambulance services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will regulations be too onerous for smaller players to invest and upgrade their existing fleet of ambulances to serve as emergency ambulances?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is certainly important, as any case of patient abuse would severely damage the trust that the public has for our healthcare industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, how will the background checks be conducted if the worker in question is a foreigner?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed licensing framework and measures under the Bill are timely and will help to strengthen Singapore's position as the premier healthcare hub of the region.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, as we transit to the new framework, it is important that we ensure that we keep regulatory costs low and not overly onerous to smaller players.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should use this as an opportunity to ambitiously widen our regulatory sandbox and tackle the tough questions on liability that will inevitably arise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Since the licensing will be services-based, should the Ministry require all licensed persons in a healthcare premises to display a photograph alongside their licence so that patients know who is who?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should we educate patients to always ask to see a licence, for example, if they are doing medical consultations online, or if they are being treated by someone other than a doctor or nurse, such as a technician operating certain equipment?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This may create a misimpression that he is a medical doctor.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Medical Services these days are getting more and more complicated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, to introduce a services-based licensing regime to replace the current premises-based one is a step towards the right direction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because, quite often, these costs will be passed on to the patients.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, how can we ensure that patients know whether the medical personnel who treat them are licensed or not?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should all medical personnel display a photograph alongside their licence?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the patient is doing online consultation, or if he is not treated by a doctor or a nurse, should the patient check the person’s licence first?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are all steps in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Member of Parliament Ms Sylvia Lim, my party Chair, has made a number of points about the Bill with which I agree and which I shall not repeat here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My speech will focus on what else can be done to contain healthcare inflation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part 57 2(R) of the Bill empowers the Minister to regulate the sector so as to require price transparency towards patients and customers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a Parliamentary reply from 2018, the Government figure for healthcare inflation measuring the growth rate of prices for healthcare-related goods and services paid by patients after Government subsidies was about 1.2% between 2013 and 2016.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Medical or healthcare inflation is a challenge faced by many countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is partly driven by the increasing availability of advanced cutting-edge drugs, treatments and diagnostic techniques which are expensive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we control medical inflation and curb any tendency towards over-treatment and over-prescription without shutting the door to research and development and innovation in the medical sphere?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the rest of my speech will focus on ideas to answer this question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will speak on several themes related to this question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The movement towards price transparency aims to make market mechanisms work to curb healthcare inflation through market competition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And prior to this, MOH has been providing similar guidance to public hospitals since 2017, I believe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Details include, depending on the type of dataset, the public or private setting, hospital ward type, bill size, operation fee, surgeon fee, anesthetist fee, facility, average length of stay and implant breakdown.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Data is in some cases published according to the 25th, 50th and 75th percentile.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is not clear what causal effect these measures have had to date of this publishing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the level of theory, a few observations can be made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not all patients would have the skill, time and inclination to study prices and make informed decisions on that basis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This problem gets compounded when that patient is faced with a medical emergency or pressing problem where familiarity with one healthcare provider or physical proximity may weigh on the decision more than any prior study of pricing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, many patients may be confused as to the link between pricing and quality and may not only be willing to pay more for better quality but may misunderstand higher pricing to mean higher quality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many patients who are more broadly consumers may use price as a surrogate for quality in the absence of other information.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help patients make the link between price and quality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am aware that this needs an investment in data systems and expertise to capture data well and risk-adjust to take into account the differential complexity of patients.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Doctors need to be reassured the system is fair or everyone will start to turn away or decline to treat complex or poor pre-morbid patients.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it could well be worth the investment and, at the very least, should be studied since what we want is value and this means price or fees as a function of outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And can such price comparisons be made a mandatory part of the financial counselling?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under pressure of time or stress, a patient may not shop around when initially choosing a healthcare service provider.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this idea may give them some food for thought for considering their healthcare service provider the next time they have the same complaint.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I turn to mechanisms to curb over-treatment and over-testing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be a natural tendency to over-prescribe, over-treat or over-test, in lieu of strong controls and pressures from customers and regulators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Earlier, I touched on how patients, as customers, may not always be in the best position, be well-incentivised or sufficiently resourced to exert pressure on healthcare providers to keep prices in check in a skillful way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insurance coverage may also distort choices by both providers and patients.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH's Agency of Care Effectiveness has been issuing care and drug guidance since 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, defining over-treatment is notoriously complex, as some cases require more extensive – and expensive – testing and treatment than others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, can we do more to monitor and publish trends relevant to curbing unnecessary treatment by focusing on specific kinds of procedures?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Italy has similar financial incentives to hospitals with lower C-section rates and publishes information on C-section rates at different hospitals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same report details how Denmark, Sweden, the United Kingdom and Finland have high day surgery rates for a number of common procedures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Studies have shown that day surgery can reduce the cost of surgical procedures substantially compared to in-patient surgery.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The report states: "In Sweden, one of the main factors that has contributed to the expansion of day surgery over the past few decades has been clinical leadership in the adoption of evidence-based guidelines to streamline pre- and post-operative surgical procedures and promote safe and effective use of day surgery.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nationwide collaboration and support from national authorities have helped to set up and disseminate new standards, while leaving sufficient autonomy to enable adaptation to local circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can be done initially by focusing on procedures where there is the most volume vis-à-vis potential to impact on cost.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue of day-surgery or outpatient surgery is a good case in point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would seem that only medical care is covered by insurance, and patients then have to pay out-of-pocket for transport, home nurse visits, perhaps some tele-monitoring and even meals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can insurance funding models be changed such that cash is paid to cover these costs pegged to but not equal to what it would have cost to do this on an inpatient basis, so as to incentivise outpatient surgery?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, ambulatory or outpatient surgery centres need a formal arrangement with the hospital for transfer in case of adverse events.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In terms of the regulatory regime, is there a sufficient nudge for hospitals to embrace ambulatory care for surgery?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask if the MOH's Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) looks into flagging out cases that, for want of a better term, can be termed "unnecessary innovation".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, an NPR article from 2017 in the United States (US) recounts how one pharmaceutical producer marketed a single pill that combined two over-the-counter (OTC) drugs as an innovation because it was easier to take one pill than two.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A month's supply of the two inexpensive drugs cost about $40.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I will turn to the promotion of generics and biosimilars.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the Mercer Marsh study quoted earlier, it was noted that Singapore's medical inflation is partially driven up by supply-led factors, such as high-cost pharmaceuticals and biologics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I asked a Parliamentary Question on the use of generics in the public healthcare system last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reply stated that, and I quote, "In 2017, to better guide institutions and doctors in the use of generic drugs, we introduced a basket of clinically and cost-effective generic drugs, which can replace a more expensive branded equivalents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH and the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) monitor new generic drugs that enter the local market and add them to the basket on a regular basis." I have two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Alternatively, a simple app or website could provide information on HSA-approved generics in respect of differential pricing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One expert at an event in Singapore on healthcare costs said that waste in OECD countries amounts to as much as one-fifth of healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has long known that many drugs remain safe and potent for years longer than their published expiration dates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: FDA and the US Department of Defense created the Shelf Life Extension Program (SLEP) to test the stability of drugs in the federal government stockpiles and then extend their expiration dates where justifiable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each of them had their expiration dates extended on average by more than four years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the same type of drugs in hospitals or pharmacies get thrown away when they expire.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does our healthcare system destroy significant quantities of drugs due to expiry?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, could we consider something like that US Shelf Life Extension Program, to use clinical data to extend the life of drugs?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is a progressive move which will cater to new models of healthcare delivery, in tandem with medical technology advancement, the growing needs of an ageing population and increased chronic disease concerns.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This augmented Bill will provide improved patient safety in the changing healthcare landscape through more efficient governance while allowing for new and innovative healthcare services to be deployed on online and mobile platforms.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I ask if the Minister will elaborate on the future plans and timeline as to when these aspects will be covered because it may affect healthcare professionals practising in these areas, or perhaps under what kind of circumstances will an actionable response be considered to include them in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, I would like to ask how MOH plans to transit healthcare institutions from the PHMCA to the HCS Act.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How will the existing services be mapped out and what will be the differences in standard requirements as well as the impact on healthcare institutions and professionals?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How will the consequences affect licensed sites which are currently co-locating with the non-licensed services, such as Traditional, Complementary and Alternative medicines or Allied Health services?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister explain the rationale for this exclusion and how can we be assured that healthcare services not governed under this Bill will provide similar patient safety and governance standards, for example, ambulance services provided by SCDF and medical services provided by the Ministry of Defence?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Would an inclusion instead enhance safety and align standards across the country, with MOH providing an independent oversight as a Ministry with expertise in healthcare?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Also, Part 2 of clause 22 requires that the Director keep and maintain a register of licensees.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Part 3 of clause 28 in the Bill imposes restrictions on licensees who employ staff to work in healthcare services which cater for the frail and vulnerable patient groups.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: What is to be done if the existing staff do not meet the current requirements stated in the new Bill?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Public Sector Data Security Review Committee chaired by Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean has made five key recommendations to improve public sector data security, and these include enhancing technology and the relevant processes to protect public data, strengthening data detection and responsiveness to data incidents by building data security competencies across the Public Service, ensuring improved accountability and transparency and, lastly, sustainability of data security efforts.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare my interest as the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few queries regarding the change from premises-based to service-based licensing for pharmacy services.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How can MOH ensure that there are no overlapping scopes and standards across different regulations?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, hospital outpatient pharmacies which provide dispensary and medication delivery services for walk-in patients, as opposed to their own hospital patients.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is the tele-pharmacy services provided in hospitals for hospital patients versus those provided by retail pharmacies for patients in the community.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Although these services are similar, they are subjected to different Acts with different licensing requirements and standards.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I seek clarification as to whether the overlapping of regulatory scopes might cause confusion and inefficiency in running these different services.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How will this impact future pharmaceutical services, such as pharmacists looking into providing vaccination service in the community?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister’s response to the above-mentioned concerns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the evolving healthcare landscape necessitates updates and changes to our licensing framework.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The refreshed structure is needed to manage new services and ensure patient safety and well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Telemedicine, an emerging area, is a field that I am particularly concerned about.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a broad field, encompassing video communications, digital storage and transmission of medical information in the form of text, data and images, remote patient monitoring, health apps on mobile devices and more.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since patients are not physically examined in person by the physicians, there is a higher risk of the doctors missing the detection of certain symptoms, resulting in misdiagnosis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As it is, it is already a challenge for the accurate detection of many illnesses and diseases as they manifest similar symptoms.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should something go wrong, how can patients seek help and redress?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will doctors be held to the same standard for telemedicine?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think it is important that medical personnel and patients have a clear understanding of their responsibilities and rights for this nascent service.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also curious whether there will be any prerequisites before a doctor can proceed with the provision of tele-medical communication.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, should the doctor and patient have a pre-existing relationship, that is, the doctor had seen the patient in a face-to-face consultation at least once before?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since patients are not physically examined in person by the physicians, there is a higher risk of the doctors missing the detection of certain symptoms, resulting in misdiagnosis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As it is, it is already a challenge for the accurate detection of many illnesses and diseases as they manifest similar symptoms.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will the Minister ensure the quality of diagnosis?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should something go wrong, how can patients seek help and redress?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will doctors be held to the same standard for telemedicine?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think it is important that medical personnel and the patients have a clear understanding of their responsibilities and their rights for this nascent service.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also curious whether there will be prerequisites before a doctor can proceed with the provision of telemedical communication.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, should the doctor and the patient have a pre-existing relationship, that is, the doctor had seen the patient in a face-to-face consultation at least once before?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Another concern is the prescription of medications.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since telemedicine can be practised wherever there is Internet connection, I would like to ask if this Bill will regulate cross-border consultations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as the Internet facilitates international trade of goods and services, will this occur in our healthcare?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can order almost everything from food to furniture, participate in courses, receive legal advice and accounting services online without taking a step out of our homes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will telemedicine proceed similarly and what controls will the Ministry put in place to protect Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to enquire about the tightening of naming restrictions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Approval will be required for terms, such as "Singapore" or "National" for new companies, but existing entities do not have to make any changes to their names.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With this, I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I commend MOH for extensive public consultation on the Bill for two years before presenting it in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have five queries and will take them in sequence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the scope of the definition of "healthcare services" under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Senior Minister of State knows, there is a wide diversity of services provided at these centres.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some focus on social well-being, which is quite clearly outside the ambit of the definition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where it gets a little more difficult is where elderly residents are offered frailty assessment, advice on physiotherapy or rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sometimes, this is done not just at centres but during house visits, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What form of assistance can be given to these organisations to help them subscribe to the new licensing regime under the HCS Bill?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, suitability of key personnel running the licensee's business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is, as the hon Senior Minister of State mentioned, to ensure that high governance standards are observed.
