speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The wording in the clause, however, introduces a subjective test because the operative word is "the opinion of the Director".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, in addition to the above requirement, under clause 23(1)(b), the licensee must also ensure that the composition of key appointment holders satisfies the skills and competencies requirements prescribed or specified in a code of practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, for the appointment of a Principal Officer (PO) or Clinical Governance Officer (CGO) under clause 24, there is no requirement imposed to ensure that these officers are suitable in the opinion of the Director.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Clause 23(2) would allow the Director to direct a licensee to remove a key appointment holder who he is satisfied is either: (a) not suitable; or (b) does not possess the skills or competencies prescribed or specified.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How will licensees be given notice of the Director's approach to the issue of suitability?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How will appeals to the Minister on such decisions under clause 48 be determined?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the Minister be able to revisit the issue de novo?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or should he decide based on the reasonableness of the Director’s opinion, even though he may personally disagree with it?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, how does the Bill assist in relation to ensuring that licensees adhere to reasonable levels of corporate governance and financial management to ensure that the entities are going concerns?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is it contemplated that the principal officer or key appointment holders take personal responsibility?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the case in the financial services industry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State made reference to essential services in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the financial services industry, they have a senior manager's regime and key appointment holders have specific responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or will it be a licensing condition imposed on the licensee?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fourth, Exclusion of Traditional Medicine, Complementary and Alternative Medicine from licensing requirements under the proposed HCS Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from the Senior Minister of State that the decision is made on a risk-based assessment, not to license these practitioners at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that the traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practitioners continue to be regulated under the TCM Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, there are other disciplines of traditional medicine, such as homeopathy or Ayurvedic medicine, which are not currently regulated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Bringing Traditional Medicine, Complementary and Alternative Medicine within the HCS regulatory framework may promote integration of services with mainstream medicine which may be beneficial to patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State mentioned that the industry would be monitored on a risk-based approach going forward.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggest the enlarging of the monitoring to also include an assessment of the potential for providing integrated services to patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that during the consultation phase, there were fears expressed that there could be increased regulatory burden and fees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, should it not be recovered from the licensees?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill is timely in view of the developments and breakthroughs in the medical sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technological advances are accelerating changes in how our healthcare services are delivered and the types of treatments available.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The updated legislative framework will enable the Ministry to better govern our healthcare sector and ensure quality of care.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have only one concern for this Bill and this is regarding NEHR.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this will ensure continuity in terms of treatment for patients and allow medical professionals to have a holistic grasp of their health conditions, there are also potential downsides.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The consequence of such a mistake may be serious, leading to more issues down the line.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Previously, PHMCA was the principal Act governing the regulation of clinics and hospitals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it worked in a time where medical services were bound by space and time, an expanded regime is necessary with the advent of telemedicine and other similar healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though there is increased flexibility in the kinds of services that can be packaged under a licence, clause 29 prevents the public from being misled by the name of the healthcare service provider.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, as evinced by the First Schedule, not all healthcare services are licensable healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is important to protect those who may use or need such services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this period of transitioning from the old regime to the new regime, how will the Ministry help healthcare providers whose services straddle, for some time, the old and new regime?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this modular services-based system provides more flexibility, compliance with regulations may become more difficult as licensees need to look through more regulations to know which are applicable to them and which are not.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The exercise may also increase the time needed to scan through a code of practice to pick up and implement relevant or salient points.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part 3 of the Bill also sets out positions the licensee has to have, that is, the PO and CGO.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The requirements for these will be set out in the code of practice per clause 23(1)(b).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does the new system compare with the current system?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister please explain the rationale and thinking behind the structure and change to this governance model?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, in the course of my work as a lawyer, which I now declare, I have worked alongside Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) of hospitals.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They have much to deal with in the day-to-day running of the hospital and regularly attend to unprecedented situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given their plate is already so full, I would ask MOH not to require that the CEO of the hospital be the PO or the CGO, and that the CEO be able, if appropriate, to delegate the role to a suitably qualified colleague.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, will current licensees with leaner manpower, such as general practitioners, struggle to meet this criterion?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides changing the mode of regulation from locale to services-based, this Bill also puts in place measures to ensure the quality of care provided.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are three committees mentioned in this Bill – the quality assurance committee, service review committee and the clinical ethics committee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The quality assurance committee is also present under PHMCA.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sections 11(3) to 11(5) of that Act are similar to clauses 51(3) to (5) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It provides that the quality assurance committee is not competent nor compellable to disclose information in Court or produce documents requested or produced solely for the purpose of the quality assurance committee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This appears to be a form of privilege which protects information and reports, preventing them from being used in medical negligence lawsuits, for instance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The quality assurance committee needs to be able to assess the true state of affairs with candidness and transparency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provision allows healthcare service providers to be candid with them and work together with them to ensure that healthcare attains a degree of standard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As this committee is not novel, would the Minister share with us how well these committees have worked in the past regime and what can be done to improve its function in the new regime?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 26 requires a case to be referred to a clinical ethics committee where a patient is recommended to go for a service in a prescribed category.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To prevent committee-shopping, clauses 26(3) and (4)(b) specify that a person must not provide the proposed prescribed service if any clinical ethics committee to which the individual’s case is referred is not satisfied that it is ethically appropriate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides having committees, another measure designed to protect the public in the provision of healthcare services is step-in orders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This order by the Minister allows partial or total takeover to protect the public's interest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the powers are intrusive and the threat of a step-in being invoked pre-emptively can cause uncertainty for all involved, would the Minister provide some examples to illustrate the severity involved in circumstances of public interest?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition to the committees and the possibility of step-in orders, the Codes of Practice provided for under clause 38 allow for greater flexibility.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is particularly valuable where technology is rapidly changing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important where the data or information is stored electronically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because in such circumstances, human assistance through the provision of passwords can greatly aid the speed and ease of accessing important information, allowing for better enforcement with less resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Healthcare services are often not "good to have" but necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will address the various issues raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There have been several questions on the regulatory scope and the types of services that will be licensed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill seeks to be clear and transparent in the scope of "healthcare services" that can be regulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai has asked if community-led initiatives, including those provided by VWOs, will be in scope and be licensed under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But sometimes, these centres also provide services that are clinical in nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, they might have a doctor located within the senior centre, and if the doctor is engaged to provide clinical services in that centre, then that doctor will require a medical clinic licence or will have to be employed by a clinic licensee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Irene Quay, Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Melvin Yong asked for timelines on the licensing of allied health, mental health and traditional medicine services, as well as non-doctor-led home and community-based services, so that the providers would have sufficient time to prepare for regulation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, the framework for any regulation, even for these services which are yet to be in scope, will be as set out in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, they will know the parameters and the landscape and rubric of the Bill, even before it applies to them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We do not, at present, have any plans to license these services but will closely monitor the landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If significant patient risks, for example, emerge in these services, then we can decide to license these services, but as I said at the outset, the broad framework will already be as set out in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, before we move to regulate any new services, Members can be assured that MOH will engage and consult with the relevant stakeholders on the proposed standards to ensure that they are contextualised for that particular service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we might have the framework set out in this Bill, but for the particular types of services and spectrum of different services, the precise way in which they will come in might have to be contextualised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we will have a programme to engage and to consult, before they are added into scope.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Irene Quay has asked why Government entities like SCDF-owned ambulances and SAF medical centres are excluded from the Bill's scope.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned at the outset, these entities serve critical national functions, and they do themselves come under separate internal governance structures and standards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add that Government entities providing healthcare services are subject to stringent internal standards and, in some cases, more stringent than what is being proposed by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SCDF serves highly-critical cases and they hold their services to higher standards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SCDF mandates a six-monthly paramedic skills certification test and quarterly Continual Professional Education sessions to improve and also broaden the knowledge, skills and competence of their emergency medical services crew.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast, the draft ambulance Regulations require Emergency Ambulance Service Crew to attend lectures, simulation, practical sessions or clinical discussions at least once every six months and paramedics are required to be recertified every two years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For SAF clinics, all personnel are qualified according to national requirements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Medical officers are trained to national standards, and are also Singapore Medical Council (SMC)-registered with working experience in the restructured hospitals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are regular refresher courses for staff, as well as regular audits for the clinics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for clarifications on how this new framework might deal with Third Party Administrators (TPAs) and medical concierges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The current scope is limited to regulating providers of direct healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: TPAs and concierge services are principally administrative in nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, MOH is monitoring the patient safety risks and studying the landscape of these services further, before deciding on the appropriate framework, if any, to regulate these entities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the licensing of TPAs and concierge services in some form is found to be needed, an amendment to the scope of this Bill can be made at the appropriate juncture to include them, again, with the appropriate contextualisation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the meantime, professional guidelines, such as the SMC's Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines (ECEG), provide guidance for medical practitioners contracting with TPAs to ensure the objectivity of the medical practitioner's clinical judgement and the provision of the required standard of care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for Members who are familiar with ECEG, you will know that advertisements are prohibited, save for certain circumstances set out; and at the end of the day, the judgement of the medical practitioner – how he looks at the patient, how he treats the patient – should be unimpaired and unaffected by any TPAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Medical practitioners are ultimately responsible for their agents, if any; and if TPAs advertise licensable healthcare services, they would be subject to clause 31 of the Bill and can only advertise on a licensee's authorisation and must comply with all relevant advertising rules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Irene Quay also raised an issue on possible overlaps between the different Acts and cited an example of hospital pharmacies being subject to both the current PHMCA and, in future, this Bill, as well as the Health Products Act (HPA).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: HPA governs the position when a pharmacy serves walk-in customers or walk-in patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such a situation, where the patient is not coming from the hospital where he would have had a prescription and had been seen by doctors, different standards would apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, we would expect that different standards should apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The pharmacy would not need a separate one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, I have taken on board Ms Irene Quay's comments about the rationalisation, and MOH and HSA will continue to streamline our processes to seek to avoid duplicative work by licensees to comply with the requirements of both this Bill as well as HPA, including for tele-pharmacy services, and will no doubt consult with Ms Irene Quay and the Society further on this point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to give an example to Ms Irene Quay, the 2019 Singapore Standard for Supply and Delivery of Medication is a common national standard for all healthcare providers and retail pharmacies if they want to supply and deliver medications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Ms Joan Pereira's questions on telemedicine, we should view telemedicine as an extension of the practice of medicine, provided through a platform different from the traditional clinic setting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nonetheless, this is the practice of medicine, and it remains regulated by existing standards, such as ECEG.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, the National Telemedicine Guidelines set out specific guidelines relevant to telemedicine that registered doctors and healthcare professionals would have to abide by.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would reiterate that the broad principle is that doctors are expected to provide the same quality and standard of care as in-person medical care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The fact that there is now, or there could be, a more convenient medium by which the care is delivered or the patient has communicated with, should not be a reason in itself to lower that standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The doctor should clearly indicate the limitations, in an appropriate case, of the telemedicine services at the start of the consultation and might, in fact, need also to refer that patient to a face-to-face consultation if he forms the view that he is unable to take proper history, to assess the patient properly and to form a sufficient judgement in order to discharge his expected standard of care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moving forward, we will continue to refine the telemedicine regulations, have them tested, looked at and assessed in the context of the industry as well, to make sure that they are as appropriate and as relevant to the ground practice as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will not only ensure that we remain in tandem with the practice of telemedicine, but that patient safety and welfare would also be adequately safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some Members have asked about cross-border healthcare services, including the use of telemedicine.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is, of course, this question of how do you enforce and how do you deal with potentially errant providers who exist outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will continue to improve patient engagement and education on the benefits and some of the obvious limitations of telemedicine, including consuming healthcare services provided from abroad where, as I have said, oversight and regulatory enforcement are not as readily available so that patients will know they can make an informed decision as to which healthcare services to use or to consume for their treatment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Melvin Yong raised questions on licensing for new healthcare services, cutting-edge healthcare services, like through the use of AI.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH is, of course, aware of the increasing role and importance of AI in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is nonetheless an evolving area, and we are monitoring this space closely and also engaging the relevant stakeholders – those who develop the AI, those who use the AI – to try to find the best possible guidelines and also to develop them in tandem with the industry to assure patient safety.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Melvin Yong made valid suggestions on the prospect of expanding the regulatory sandbox to these cutting-edge areas to explore new frontiers and to test the boundaries, and to see what works and what does not work in the safe context of the sandbox.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will do so, so that we can then introduce these regulations after they have been found to be workable and, most importantly, safe for the patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moving on to the private ambulance sector, Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Melvin Yong raised questions about this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Melvin Yong mentioned, it is an area that was not previously regulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As such, progressive efforts have been made to ensure that private ambulance operators will be able to ramp up and be regulated under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point is, if overnight, everyone is subject to this Bill, you might then find, as I think one of the Members mentioned, some questions as to whether every ambulance operator will be able to deliver the same level of services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we take a more gradated and calibrated approach on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2017, we issued standards for emergency ambulance and medical transport services so that operators will have clarity on the regulatory requirements that they must meet.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This process, where we expect to see ambulance operators come into scope in the second phase, in fact, started some years ago so as to socialise these requirements to them, to acclimatise them to the standards that they would have to meet.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH recognises that private operators may require support to ramp up their capabilities and to meet these standards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, a year later, in 2018, the Voluntary Accreditation Scheme (VAS), which Ms Sylvia Lim referred to in her speech, was launched to help familiarise private operators with the applicable standards for clinical governance, for personnel, and also for vehicles early, so that steps can be taken to raise the clinical service standards, and they know what the benchmark and the bar would be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, training schemes have also been introduced and facilitated by MOH to upskill the existing manpower to meet the new requirements for paramedics and also emergency medical technicians.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will continue to work with other operators to prepare their vehicles, as well as skilling up their manpower.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Ms Sylvia Lim asked questions about costs and fees of private ambulance operators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Melvin Yong have asked how the Bill impacts existing PHMCA licensees and whether its requirements to enhance governance will place an unnecessary burden on licensees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will, of course, know that that is not the intention of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the same time, healthcare services, especially those that are newer, will need to be properly regulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The rationale for introducing the enhanced governance requirements is to ensure that the licensees are well managed, so that they can effectively and safely serve their patients' needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, we recognise that the scale and complexity of licensees and the kind of services that they offer, the scale of their operations and their set-up will differ.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The requirements will, therefore, be attenuated to take into account the nature of the licensee's business, so as not to unnecessarily increase regulatory burden on all of them in equal proportions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill requires all licensees to appoint a Principal Officer (PO), and certain licensees providing more complex and technical services must also appoint a Clinical Governance Officer (CGO).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The PO is akin to the manager appointed by the licensee under the present PHMCA regime and is responsible to assist the licensee in ensuring compliance with the requirements of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The PO is required to have sufficient organisational authority and management skills to adjust operations and make decisions, while the CGO is intended to oversee the technical and clinical aspects of the service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will be satisfied as long as the PO and CGO are able to discharge their duties appropriately and we will not require specific personnel, such as the CEO, to be the PO or CGO in each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similarly, for small GP clinics that likely do not provide any complex specialised services, one individual can fill the role of the licensee and the PO, and a separate CGO will also not be required in those cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai queried on whether there are objective criteria to determine the suitability of key appointment holders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai would have seen clause 2(3) of the Bill which sets out the factors that will be considered in deciding whether a person is suitable to be appointed as a key appointment holder, PO or CGO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It provides what I would regard as the no-fly zones, the broader outliers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is financial suitability, there is the question of whether there is a prior conviction, antecedents and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the same time, we also do not want to be overly prescriptive in the quality of the candidate that comes forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to that extent, there is an interplay between the criteria that are set up here and what the Director of Medical Services might subjectively determine as to their suitability in each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also intend to provide clear guidance of instances where persons will be found to be unsuitable, so that licensees will be apprised of the applicable criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This can be done through regulations and, as Members know, clause 38 of the Bill also provides for a Code of Practice as regards the relevance of all licensees to these requirements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It can be published in the Code as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Should a licensee appeal to the Minister against any decision to reject the appointment of his key appointment holders, the PO or CGO, the Minister will consider each case based on its own facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Murali Pilliai raised the point about the appeal and how the Minister will consider it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for Mr Murali Pillai's point on ensuring that key appointment holders are competent in corporate governance and financial management, we agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the reason really to ensure there is a PO and a CGO that deal with the technical and clinical aspects of the practice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And MOH plans to include such requirements in the Code of Practice, as I have said, under clause 38 of this Bill, which will guide licensees with a bit more specificity on the levels of skill and competencies required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I have said, at the same time, not being overly prescriptive so that it becomes something that you just have to tick all the boxes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Prof Fatimah Lateef have asked for details on specified committees for quality assurance and clinical ethics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I believe Ms Sylvia Lim also raised questions on the quality assurance committees (QACs).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They provide a protected environment, as Mr Christopher de Souza said, without prejudice, for healthcare professionals to be open about an adverse event to identify the problems, learn from it, and correct errors without fear of being sued based on the materials that are discussed there or the discussions or candid sharing at those occasions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through the learning environment that the QACs foster, proper root-cause analysis can be conducted and professionals can come up with solutions that will prevent the recurrence of such errors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the years, QACs have served their functions well in reviewing adverse clinical events.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked specifically on the functioning of the QACs – how they are performing, and whether, ultimately, they will provide proper oversight of the way in which procedures are handled or the way in which patients might then raise complaints.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think I heard Ms Sylvia Lim mentioned also the case of Prof Lim that went before the Court of three Judges a few months ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The QACs' function is in reviewing adverse clinical events and recommending initiatives to improve the quality and the standard of care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is quite different, and it does not affect the other avenues available to a patient, either through SMC's disciplinary proceedings or, should the need arise, for civil compensation under the civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those still exist and nothing in this Bill prejudices that or changes the options available to a patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, the oversight of a case or oversight of professional misconduct or conduct of a medical practitioner still falls with the SMC, and the rubric and the regime that are there still exist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The QACs exist separately and, as I have explained, for a different purpose and outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Clinical Ethics Committees (CECs) have a different role to play.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To give some examples to Members of what we have in mind, for instance, where there is a proposed surgical separation of conjoined twins, that will be something that the CEC should review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Or, for example, in the creation of a saviour sibling to save one sibling, that should also be considered by the CEC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are relevant matters that fall within the rubric of both clinical as well as ethical considerations that the CEC would be well-placed to review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me talk about the step-in mechanisms and employment restrictions which various Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned at the outset, the rationale for these powers is, ultimately, to protect patients and ensure that they receive not only appropriate but also continual care, notwithstanding the performance of the healthcare service provider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Louis Ng raised queries as to when the step-in powers could be triggered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will be triggered when it is in the patients' interests to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other alternative measures as may be appropriate in the circumstances – like penalties or warnings if the situation is not at a sufficiently grave stage, or the appointment of a new management team to rectify the issues – these are measures which could be considered, and within reason, before a step-in order is made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These powers can make a real difference in protecting patient safety and ensuring the continuity of care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, there may be cases of certain specified service providers with financial difficulties who may find it difficult to afford to continue its services and patient care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, in turn, translates into undermining the safety of patients and adversely affecting their welfare.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members would know that under the existing PHMCA, MOH can only take regulatory actions, such as revoking or suspending the licence, which was not feasible, given that this would interrupt continuity of care for the resident patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the Bill, step-in powers will now enable MOH to intervene in the operations instead to address the problems and improve continuity of care for patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will also "step-out" once the service is stabilised and patient safety is assured.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The objective of the check is to prevent individuals who have committed egregious crimes – it might be causing hurt, grievous hurt, or more serious crimes like rape – from being employed and potentially harming vulnerable patients in these settings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For foreigners – and I think some Members asked about the efficacy of this regime for foreigners – the background check really would have to be on a best-efforts basis, as and when information arises and can be determined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have asked for an update on the measures, including cybersecurity measures, to assist licensees in protecting health information in their electronic medical records.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Ms Irene Quay also asked when MOH would be mandating contribution of patient health information to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think one of the Members calls it the "elephant in the room" that is actually not in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, indeed, it is not in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, clause 27 of the Bill requires licensees to implement measures to protect their medical records and ensure that the records are accurate and remain up to date.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As MOH encourages more licensees to digitalise their medical records, we will also be working closely with the licensees to study further ways to safeguard the collection, storage, access, use and, of course, sharing of health information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for NEHR, Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked if this would represent a mortal blow to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, nonetheless, MOH will want to ensure that all necessary safeguards are in place to handle the evolving cybersecurity threats and also ensure that where various cybersecurity reviews for NEHR have been commissioned, the appropriate enhancements would be made to the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will make further announcements on this at the appropriate juncture.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me turn to queries raised by Prof Fatimah Lateef and Ms Irene Quay on the co-location between licensed and unlicensed services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I explained at the opening speech, the prohibition on the co-location is to prevent parties from being misled into consuming the unlicensed services under the impression that it is part and parcel or adjunct to the licensed services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is no different from the current position under the present PHMCA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, where the services are complementary to each other between the licensed and the unlicensed services, some examples I mentioned earlier, this concern is mitigated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in these circumstances, we will be prepared to make an exception for certain healthcare professionals to co-locate with licensees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, a physiotherapist can co-locate with an orthopaedic clinic, so that more holistic services can be provided, such as in that case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other circumstances, we will review on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill also contains other measures which will assist patients in making informed decisions when selecting healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, Ms Irene Quay cited the register of licensees in clause 22 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This register will be accessible by the public, making it easy to check, for them to determine if a provider is, in fact, licensed by MOH or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Melvin Yong asked how we can prevent patients from being misled by unqualified providers into thinking that they are qualified when they are not and then go and seek their services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First of all, the licensee is responsible for ensuring that their personnel, all their personnel, are appropriately qualified and competent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a licensee permits unqualified personnel to provide healthcare services, MOH could investigate and take the appropriate regulatory actions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, clause 31 plays a part by limiting advertising of licensable healthcare services to licensees only and, as I mentioned at the start, to persons acting on the authority of a licensee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, clause 37 allows MOH to publish information to ensure patient welfare, or for public interest, and this includes publishing a list of unlicensed providers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, ultimately, public education will play an important role to prevent or reduce and, as far as possible, remove all of such misimpressions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH has and will be enhancing efforts, as we implement the Bill, for public education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When in doubt, I would advise patients to check on the registers maintained by the professional boards, such as SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Melvin Yong raised a query on the regulation of mental health professionals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Professional associations, such as the Singapore Psychological Society and the Singapore Association for Counselling, provide advice on trained professionals in their respective fields.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the scenario that Mr Melvin Yong is trying to avoid, where there is doubt as to whether someone is a counsellor or not, whether he is a psychologist or not, the associations can provide further avenues for assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Prof Fatimah Lateef have given useful comments on other Bill requirements, such as naming restrictions and point-of-care tests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, of course, that will have to be revisited if they either sell the business or change the ownership in a material way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me turn to healthcare costs which several Members, including Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Mr Leon Perera, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Christopher de Souza, have raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Concerns regarding the impact of the Bill on healthcare costs and, of course, passing on of these costs to the patients were raised, and I think those were valid concerns.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For now, let me just very quickly outline the various initiatives that have been done to keep healthcare costs low and sustainable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I had mentioned, we adopt a multi-tiered approach – multi-tiered, multi-pronged, and I would say also multifaceted approach – to controlling costs, with the basic assurance that no Singaporean would be denied access to basic healthcare due to financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the assurance that would be given.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The multi-tiered approach that we take will include enhancing the 3Ms – which we have done at various stages and which we will continue to do – MediSave, MediShield Life and MediFund; and also extending significant subsidies, including the CHAS scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also put in place other measures to curb the increase in healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leon Perera no doubt has cited a number of different studies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At various juncture, he mentioned studies from various places, data published from various sources, some experts speaking at a conference, delivering a paper and some results from programmes and studies somewhere.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not prepared at this stage to agree to the conclusion of these studies because they need to be contextualised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We need to look at who studied it and what the assumptions might be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Mr Leon Perera would be happy to share these studies and the other details that he had mentioned in his speech with us, we can do a more careful study and look at the options open in terms of adopting some of these measures in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But where we are on common ground between Mr Leon Perera and the Bill, is the need to ensure that we promote price transparency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Leon Perera mentioned at the outset, indeed, that is specifically provided for in the Regulations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all these factors, they operate dynamically and they all have to be taken into account, depending on the nature of the service that has to be delivered and, of course, the patient's safety and the requirements of each individual patient as well.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong, are you likely to wrap up within the next five minutes?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To give one example, to reduce the administrative workload for all existing providers as we implement the Bill, MOH conducted extensive stakeholder engagements – part of what we did in that two years leading up to the preparation of this Bill – to understand and do a deep dive of their licensing needs and map these, as far as possible, to the new Bill licences and the requirements in this new regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH will continue to provide clear instructions and appropriate channels for stakeholders to ask questions, clarify their doubts or come and seek assistance from us on the transition to the new regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Various Members – Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Christopher de Souza, Ms Irene Quay, Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Melvin Yong and also Dr Lee Bee Wah – have asked how this Bill impacts operating costs and, in particular, whether licensees will pay more fees as a result of the new landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, let me assure the House, and I think one of the Members said, and I echo that, that this is not intended as a revenue-generating mechanism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is necessary because of the measures that I have set out in the opening speech, that the new regulatory landscape is necessary to deal with evolving changes to the healthcare landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The general principle is that licence fees are pegged at a level commensurate with the cost of manpower and resources incurred from the expected inspections and the audits to be done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH has and will continue to streamline our licensing processes to keep our regulatory costs down, as well as reduce excessive regulatory burden on licensees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is really no reason or basis for providers to pass on any of these costs to patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The remaining providers who will see an increase are mainly providers who will be providing new licensable services regulated under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will space out as far as possible the increase, spread it out over three renewal cycles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill introduces a regulatory regime that is sufficiently nimble and flexible to protect patient safety and welfare, but at the same time, take on board the rapidly evolving changes to the healthcare landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, it will accommodate new healthcare services, new care models and also nurture innovation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will ensure that healthcare services provided in Singapore will be able to address the existing and also the future needs of our population.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Well done, Senior Minister of State, you have kept it within five minutes.
